title: Transport regimes in tunnel ferromagnetic Josephson junctions
authors: R. Satariano, A. A. Golubov, E. Raja, R. Ferraiuolo, F. Calloni, H. G. Ahmad, A. Vettoliere, N. Poccia, L. Parlato, G. Ausanio, C. Granata, G. P. Pepe, M. Yu. Kupriyanov, F. Tafuri, D. Montemurro, D. Massarotti
abstract: We present a systematic study of the temperature-dependent transport properties of Nb- and Al-based superconductor--insulator--thin superconductor--ferromagnet--superconductor (SIsFS) Josephson junctions. By varying the superconducting material and the thickness of the intermediate superconducting layer, we identify three distinct transport regimes: a tunnel-dominated SIS-like regime, a temperature-driven crossover, and a complex weak-link regime. A unified Usadel-based description connects these regimes through the self-consistent pair potential of the intermediate s-layer. While for Al-based devices an SIS-like transport regime is observed, a self-consistent calculation of the s/F/S proximity electrode, combined with perturbative tunnel coupling to the outer electrode, accounts for Nb devices with different thickness of the superconducting interlayer. The calculation places the 10-nm-interlayer sample in a proximity-supported, strongly suppressed s state, close to the SInFS limit in which the interlayer is effectively driven normal (\textit{n}). A reduced nonlinear long-junction description captures the same limiting physics. The evolution of I_cR_N(T) thereby provides a direct experimental signature of the three transport regimes. Beyond the fundamental interest, the results establish practical design guidelines: Nb junctions with sufficiently thick s interlayers are well suited for high-speed cryogenic memory elements and tunable superconducting parametric amplifiers, while Al junctions are natural candidates for coherent superconducting quantum circuits
summary: This paper systematically studies transport in SIsFS Josephson junctions using both experiment and advanced theory. It identifies three distinct operational regimes—tunnel, crossover, and weak-link—governed by the intermediate superconducting layer. The findings establish practical guidelines for using these junctions in cryogenic memory and quantum circuits.
main_problem: The study systematically investigates the temperature-dependent transport properties in complex superconductor-insulator-thin superconductor-ferromagnet-superconductor (SIsFS) Josephson junctions.
main_result: The research identifies three distinct transport regimes—tunnel-dominated, crossover, and weak-link—and provides design guidelines showing Nb junctions are suitable for memory while Al junctions are better for quantum circuits.
method: The work combines experimental measurements (I-V curves, $I_c R_N(T)$) with a unified, self-consistent Usadel-based theoretical description.
model_or_system: The physical system is the SIsFS Josephson junction, analyzed using a dirty-limit Usadel framework that models the self-consistent pair potential across the intermediate superconducting layer.
key_observables: Current-voltage (I-V) characteristics, critical current-normal state resistance product ($I_c R_N$) vs. temperature, and the anomalous amplitude/pair potential profiles.
important_parameters: Intermediate layer thickness ($d_s$), superconducting material (Nb vs. Al), and the intrinsic interlayer pairing scale ($T^*$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a self-consistent calculation of the pair potential and uses approximations like treating the tunnel barrier coupling perturbatively.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature evolution of transport properties ($I_c R_N(T)$) across different junction types, and supplementary figures show the self-consistent profiles of the anomalous amplitude and pair potential across the s/F/SR structure.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and experimental measurements to applying a unified Usadel theory, detailing how the theory reproduces the three distinct transport regimes observed in both Al and Nb junctions.
why_interesting: The detailed modeling of proximity effects and the identification of crossover scales ($T^*$) provide rich insights into how superconducting correlations are modified by magnetic and structural interfaces, relevant to superconducting quantum devices.
